utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Mr. Karadzic, you have more questions for the remainder of your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a couple short questions to which the witness will be able to answer by yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, I take it you have heard some advice from Mr. Robinson, but it was totally inappropriate that you put several statements to the witness yesterday. Please continue then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Garic, when it comes to the Territorial Defence of Novo Sarajevo, was anything against the Law on All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And those who were organised into Territorial Defence units during that time before the arrival of the army, did any of them commit a crime that was covered up?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were cases of crimes, but none were covered up. There were subsequent court proceedings. For example, the chief of Novo Sarajevo municipality was involved in a problem but there were proceedings after that. Nothing was covered up, although there may have been crimes committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Garic, for having to testify here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, you stated that you had one question yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. Just one question that arises from the questions of the accused relating to the ethnic make-up of Novo Sarajevo. If we could have 65 ter 00242F, please, which is an extract from the 1991 census. Further cross-examination by Ms. Gustafson:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Garic, yesterday in re-direct you were asked what is the majority population --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, can you speak up? I can't hear the interpreter very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that better, Mr. Garic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked what's the majority population in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, and you answered: "In Novo Sarajevo, the population is mainly Serbian." And you also stated that the majority were Serbs, over 50 per cent of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 10 of the English and page 15 of the B/C/S in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Garic, this is from the 1991 census, and if we could zoom in on the middle of the page in B/C/S where it gives the breakdown for Novo Sarajevo. Do you see the information there for Novo Sarajevo, Mr. Garic, it's in the middle of the page? And it has information from 19 --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letters are very small.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we make those figures for Novo Sarajevo bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Garic -- there we go. That's better. There we go. Can you see them now, Mr. Garic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Is it possible to also scroll down so that the table headings can be seen. I apologise. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, we can see the ethnic breakdown for Novo Sarajevo in 1991. The first column is "total," then it's "Croat, Muslim, Serb, Yugoslav, and other." And we have numbers and percentages. And if we could go back to the previous view. That's great. Thank you. So we have 9.3 per cent Croat, 35.7 per cent Muslim, 34.6 per cent Serb, and then we have Yugoslavs and others. So contrary to what you stated yesterday, Novo Sarajevo was not over 50 per cent Serb; it was just under 35 per cent Serb, and, in fact, there were just about the same number of Muslims as Serbs as well as a significant number of Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, judging from the table that we're looking at now, yes, yes. However, it is my opinion that all those who declare themselves as Yugoslavs, they are, as a matter of fact, Serbs. That's the way I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, plenty of people in Sarajevo consider themselves to be Yugoslavs of all -- people of all ethnicities; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. However, most of them were Serbs. This is my very, very deep belief. I believe that mostly the Serbs declare themselves as Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we establish the source of this document? This is Croatia in 1995; right? Can we go back to the first page where we can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that can be clarified by Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is an extract from the 1991 census. Extracts from this document have been tendered throughout the trial. I don't think that there's been any concerns as to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the e-court explains that it is -- it was published in Zagreb in 1995. Can you see the -- could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour. I'll have to look into that. I can't comment on that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's the Republic of Croatia, state bureau of statistics, Zagreb, April 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I see that, Your Honour. I'll look into it and get back to the Court. If it could be marked for identification for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, do you object to the admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Other than verifying the provenance of it, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's written here it's Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it probably ought to be compared with the official census to make sure that we're working with the correct numbers, but short of that we don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5964, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless my colleagues have questions for you, Mr. Garic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for your coming to The Hague. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in relation to the issue raised during the private session, the Chamber will admit the cover page and the relevant page, only those two pages. That -- I think that's fine with the Prosecution as well, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's fine. And while I'm on my feet I should also mention I communicated with Mr. Robinson. We would like to tender the extracts from the witness's 2004 OTP interview that were used in cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And could you identify the page numbers that were dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's pages -- well, page 1 for the identifying information; pages 16 to 17 that were referenced at transcript page 29733 through 29734; page 26, referenced at transcript page 29650 through 29653; and page 54, referenced at transcript page 29692 and 29693; and those extracts have been uploaded under 65 ter 24038.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you not say to the effect that he dealt with his nickname in pages 47 to 52 about his nickname Momo?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check it and --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'll check --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, the Chamber is minded to include those pages as well. I take it there's no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll give a number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5965, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the next witness prepared, ready to come? Yes, let's bring him in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I request the next witness be given a warning pursuant to Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Karadzic -- Mr. Gengo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you start giving evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a particular Rule at the Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution or the accused or even from the Chamber if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the discretion to oblige you to answer the question. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My good morning applies to everybody. Good morning to everybody. And I would like to call up 1D6033.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Mr. Gengo, what was your rank when you left the army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I was lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, did you provide a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the statement, the one that is in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it read out to you and does it reflect your words correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions today to you in the courtroom, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, let us make breaks between questions and answers because we speak the same language and if we do not break between questions and answers the interpreters will not be able to interpret properly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender this statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter. I would like to tender the entire package with the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it you are also tendering three associated exhibits as well?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellencies, the package is an offer to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. They will be all admitted. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The statement 65 ter number 1D06033 will be Exhibit D2383, 65 ter number 1D10007 will be Exhibit D2384, 65 ter number 1D10008 will be Exhibit D2385, and 65 ter number 1D10009 will be Exhibit D2386.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On this occasion before I forget again, Mr. Robinson, I emphasise again to write down the exact 65 ter number in the future in order not -- for the witness -- the Chamber staff not to waste time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to read out a short summary of Lieutenant-Colonel Gengo's statement in English. [In English] From 1979 to 1991 Slavko Gengo worked as a highly skilled mechanic for the infantry weapons at the Lukavica barracks in Sarajevo garrison. In 1991 he was transferred to the 216th Mountain Brigade in Han Pijesak and appointed commander of the technical maintenance, weapons, and ammunition workshop. In September 1992 he was transferred to the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade and appointed officer for technical supplies. From January 1994 to February 1995 he was commander of the 7th Infantry Battalion of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade. From February 1995 until the end of the war he performed logistical duties in the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. On February the 5th, 1994, day of Markale I incident, he was in the command of the battalion in Hresa, 7 kilometres from Mrkovici. He did not hear any launching activities -- launcher activities nor did anyone report on that fact from his battalion. He was informed that an inspection team would come to the VRS Main Staff, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and the brigade command, escorted by UNPROFOR. The artillery pieces were not moved from their established firing positions before, during, or after the incident at Markale Market. Milorad Dzida informed Slavko Gengo about the content of the inspection and presented his conclusion that everything was fine, based on everything that had been seen. Several days later, during a UNPROFOR regular visit, the French major in charge of the sector told Slavko Gengo through an interpreter that the on-site finding indicated that the 7th Battalion had nothing to do with the incident at Markale. He first heard about the Green Berets -- Mr. Gengo first heard about the Green Berets in 1991 from the JNA commander of Muslim ethnicity. The objectives of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps units were defensive actions. Fire was opened exclusively against the enemy's combat positions and mostly as a response to their actions. Neither he nor his unit had any intention to cause civilian casualties or terrorise civilians who were under the control of the Muslim authorities. They were informed about the basic provisions of international law of war and humanitarian law through reports, orders, and the media. When required, the higher levels of command would issue orders of various forms of bans with the aim to respect international law standards. On the contrary, civilians in the zone of responsibility felt endangered. Since the area where they lived was under constant threat, their decision and intention to defend themselves was strengthened. Most members of the 7th Battalion were men who lived in the battalion's zone of responsibility, local population. They had a deficit of professional commanding officers. The battalion had four 120-millimetre mortars, two at the firing positions in Mrkovici and two at Gornje Biosko. They also had four 92 mortars, two on Debelo Brdo and two at Mrkovici. The average distance of the Muslim and Serbian lines were around 100 metres. Almost all positions from the opposing Muslim units were in settlements which were continuously inhabited by civilians. They frequently informed the UNPROFOR about abuses regarding the deployment of military targets, fire from civilian facilities, and cease-fire violations. They also had information that enemy heavy artillery, that means tanks, frequently fired from the direction of Kosevo and the tunnel at Ciglane. This forced them, the Serbs, to return fire against it. Occasionally, groups of snipers armed with sniper rifles and passive scopes would come to the zone of responsibility of the opposing units. They would fire during the night at this position and level -- and leave the area. They would also fire at the passenger buses, civilian cars, and everything else that travelled along the Vogosca-Hresa-Pale road. Local Muslim population regularly protested against their stays, because they knew that a response from the Serbian side could follow. The VRS provided security for the Mostanica spring water-supply line, made UNPROFOR's access possible, and that of the teams from Sarajevo in order to do check and repair. Water-supply was never deliberately switched off. Everyone who left Sarajevo via the Serbian positions could continue their journey as they wished. Conversely, he was aware that a large number of Serbs that remained in the area of the town under the control of the Muslim authorities were not allowed to leave the town. [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this point in time, I don't have any questions for this witness. I give the floor to my -- to Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gengo. I'm here to ask you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution. Now, Mr. Gengo, first of all, it's correct, isn't it, that you met me and two of my colleagues in the presence of a member of the Defence on the 16th of October, 2012?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You're aware that that interview was audio recorded?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you tell the truth in that interview?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, turning to another preliminary matter. As Mr. Karadzic said, your statement was taken by members of the Defence team. Could you name the members of the Defence team who took your statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I don't know which period you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm referring to the statement that you confirmed a few minutes ago which has been admitted before the Court. Could you confirm who took the initial version of that statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Savcic, Milomir took the first statement from the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And anyone else involved in that initial interview?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. Now I'm going to move to a few of the things that we discussed in our interview. First of all, the question of communications. You said there were 650 men in your battalion; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Over 800. There were 650 in the infantry companies. All the others were for logistics support. There was a technical platoon, a quartermaster platoon, medical security, medical support, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How many were in the communications section?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Fifteen men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you have communications with the Kosevo Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were they generally good, those communications?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, it functioned fairly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you also have communications with the brigade command, the corps command, with the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes, I did. With the 4th, with the brigade command, but not with the corps. I was in touch with the brigade command. I was subordinated to them and it wasn't necessary for me to communicate with the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your communications with the brigade command and with the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment were generally satisfactory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: They were satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The commander of the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment was who?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, there were two regiments in the zone of responsibility, the 4th Mixed Regiment, there was Bartla Jovan and there was the 4th MAP, and there was a certain Cvetkovic there whose name I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now in your battalion you had a mortar platoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How many were in the mortar platoon?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: It was a mortar platoon, 36 or 37 men. It depended. The number changed. It wasn't always the same number. People would leave, disappear, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you control the firing of rounds by that mortar platoon?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: They were subordinated to me. So the mortars could not be used without my authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And did you need to seek authorisation from anybody to order the firing of mortars?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I had to seek authorisation from the superior command, the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That was Colonel Lizdek?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did Colonel Lizdek have to seek authority from anyone?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I don't know about that. That didn't fall within my remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, I suggest that you told me in our interview that only with the authorisation of General Galic first and later was from General Milosevic could Lizdek approve the firing of a mortar round; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: General Galic wasn't the commander when I was the battalion commander. Dragomir Milosevic was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is it true to say that the corps commander, the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, ultimately controlled the firing of mortar rounds by your battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, he was probably privy to this. The brigade commander probably informed the corps commander. That's how the chain of command worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, did you exercise discipline over your battalion effectively?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did the mortar crews ever fire without your approval?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 18 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Gaynor. I wasn't clear about the witness's answer about the 4th Mixed Regiment and 4th MAP. Could you ask the -- could you tell us again what they are about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this concern me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. When asked about the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment you answered to the effect that there were two regiments, one is 4th Mixed Regiment, the other was 4th MAP, but it -- your answer wasn't clear so that's why I'm asking you again to tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the zone of responsibility of the 7th Battalion, there were -- there was the 4th MAP and the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment, their units were deployed there. Bartla Jovan was one of the commander. He was the command of the 4th Mixed and the commander of the 4th MAP was Cvetkovic, Radislav, but I'm not sure if that was his name. And some of the artillery was behind the lines of the 7th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you heard this but I don't remember at this moment, but what does "MAP" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mixed artillery regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you follow, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, I share your confusion, Your Honour. The -- perhaps we can ask the witness to distinguish between the role of the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment and the 4th MAP, which appears to be the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they're two different units, two different regiments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I leave it to you, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you distinguish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Before you go further, there is something I should like to have clarified, a question you'd put to the witness. General, it was put to you by Mr. Gaynor: "I suggest to you that in our interview that only with the authorisation of General Galic first and later General Milosevic could Lizdek approve the firing of a mortar." Now, your answer was: "General Galic was not the commander when I was the battalion commander. Dragomir Milosevic was the commander." But could you answer the question for me, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat that. What answer would you like me to provide?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor suggested to you that in your interview with him only with the authorisation of General Galic first and later Milosevic could Lizdek approve the firing of a mortar round. Do you agree with that, that you said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said that I believe that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: So that is the case? Did you hear me? Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, could you interpret that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, are you seeing the point I'm trying to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Can I have that question answered, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: First of all, Witness, General Galic was the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps during the period that you worked at the command of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade, more or less; isn't that true during --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: -- correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The successor to General Galic as commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was General Dragomir Milosevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, we agreed that you could only authorise the firing of a mortar with the approval of Lizdek; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And Lizdek, in turn, could only authorise the firing of a mortar with the approval of the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I assume that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Now, just going back to the earlier point about the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment, you referred to the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment and the 4th MAP. Again, could you clarify if you can what the difference was in the role of those two units or regiments?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, they differed in terms of the weapons that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain just a little more clearly what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: They differed in terms of the weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Gengo, could you clarify whether one regiment had heavier weapons perhaps than another regiment. If they were both artillery regiments, did they both have the same kinds of artillery? Did one have heavier artillery? One have lighter artillery? Could you give Their Honours some kind of indication what the difference was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, the difference was that, for example, one of them had BOVs and the other didn't. They had BOVs, and they had other types of weapons that the other unit didn't have. I'm not an artillery man, so I'm not in a position to know exactly what they had, what kind of weapons they had. So as I said, they had BOVs or APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is a BOV?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: It's an armoured personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in your statement at paragraph 18 which is to be found on page 5, you say: "Heavy weapons against our lines were mostly used from the firing positions from the sector of Kosevo below Grdonj and from the Jajce barracks." You recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, did you respond to fire coming from those locations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, I responded to fire if they attacked. It depended on whether they were attacking the road. I had a retaliate with authorisation from my command. I had to fire on the firing position that was obstructing the passage of vehicles from the town, from the municipalities of Ilijas, Hadzici, Vogosca, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'm returning to something that we discussed in our interview. Can you confirm that when you were responding to fire coming from the Kosevo area or the Jajce barracks area, that you would use 120-millimetre mortars to do so?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: 120-millimetre mortars were used only when my positions were attacked, so whether that was on the Mala Tvrdjava-Velika Tvrdjava axis that's when I used 120-millimetres that were located at Mrkovici. That was in front of the defence line Grdonj. 120-millimetre mortars that were in the Biosko-Debelo Brdo sector were ones that I used when the Faletici-Zecija Glava sectors were attacked. Those lines were lines where mortars had been placed and they weren't used on any other axis. The Jajce barracks was at that forward place on the Zmajevac hill or Sedrenik. It's all in the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We'll confirm the location of the Jajce barracks in a moment. Can you confirm that when you were responding to fire coming from the Kosevo area and the Jajce barracks area, that you used 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your statement at paragraph 13 and I think you've confirmed it a moment ago, you said you had two 120-millimetre mortar positions at Mrkovici and two 120-millimetre mortar positions at Gornje Biosko; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: That's one position, two mortars. That was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, it's in your statement. You had two 120-millimetre mortar positions at Mrkovici; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You had two more 120-millimetre mortar positions at Gornje Biosko?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure to which question witness answered "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I won't interrupt. Just tell the Judges where the four mortar positions were located.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Two mortars at Mrkovici, 120-millimetre mortars; two mortars in sector of Donje Biosko-Debelo Brdo. That's the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now could we --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: That's the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at D2385.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What's coming up now, Mr. Gengo, is a map which you marked. And at the end of paragraph 14 of your statement you said that you marked in red circles the positions of the support hardware on this map. Now, in paragraph 14 you described quite an array of support hardware. So I'd like you to identify with the assistance of the usher those circles which represent the 120-millimetre mortar positions at Mrkovici and the 120-millimetre mortar positions at Gornje Biosko. Perhaps we could zoom in on the centre part of the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid whether this is such a quality to be able to zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I think if Your Honours can see the four red circles towards the top of the map, if -- my intention was to get the witness to identify which of those refer to the 120-millimetre mortar positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, with a pen could you simply put a circle around the two locations you have described, the Mrkovici mortars and the Gornje Biosko mortars.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Is that Mrkovici? Could we zoom in so that I can see a little more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Usher, would you mind zooming in on the top part of this map for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I? Mrkovici, Mrkovici is here. This is Biosko.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you put an M next to Mrkovici and a B next to Biosko, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, could you sign and date that, please. Could you put your signature and -- oh, it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I tender that, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5966, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, you know where the Jajce barracks are, don't you? You were there in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You'd be able to identify their position on a map or would you like me to remind you of its location?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to. I can't see it very well. I know that it is in the city on the slope of a hill. It's difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I call up, please, P2193. It's P2193, please. Now, in this map we can see on the far left the Kosevo area, to the middle on the far left, and then I think that's fairly visible. If we look down towards the bottom right towards a box marked with the English word "legend," could we zoom in on the bottom right corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you see near where there's a bend in the river to the left of the box marked "legend," there's a building with the figure "103" marked in red. The building looks like a very large capital E. Do you see it, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you confirm that is the Jajce barracks?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, we'll move now to a another map, please, and that is -- first of all, we'll look at P1021.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, this is a map showing confrontation lines and VRS assets around the city of Sarajevo. Perhaps we can go in, blow up a little bit towards the city of Sarajevo, please. That's perfect. Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Witness, you see the Cyrillic letters "SRK" marking the area of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And to the east of that you see the Cyrillic letters "DK" marking the area of the Drina Corps. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, your brigade's area of responsibility extended from the north-eastern edge of the front line all the way towards the territory held by the Drina Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes, if we're talking about the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, your brigade. Now -- so your brigade had a front on the edge of the city of Sarajevo and behind that it was free territory as far as the Drina Corps, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to take you to a blown-up version of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And could I ask the Registrar, please, for 65 ter 23919E, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just to confirm my earlier question where I said the expression "free territory," we both understand that to mean territory controlled by the Bosnian Serb army; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in this map, if I can ask the Registrar to blow it up a little, we see -- you'll see in a moment the areas of Kosevo and Grdonj. If we can blow up the central part of the map, please. Are you able to see the words "Kosevo" yet?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now you also see the area where we identified the Jajce barracks just above the bend in the river. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And do you see the word "Grdonj" on this map?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just so it's clear for everyone, I'd like to ask the court usher, please, to help you just to circle, if you will, the word "Kosevo," circle the word "Grdonj," and then identify the location of the Jajce barracks.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Grdonj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, please. Circle the word "Kosevo," please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Kosevo is a wider area as a matter of fact. The term denotes a wider area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Circle the area which you understand to mean the Kosevo area.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, no. I believe that this area below, that would be ... I don't see the brick works Kobilja Glava, Pionirska Dom, all those things are in the Kosevo sector. That also includes the Kosevo stadium. I would say that it is this part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gengo, the word "Kosevo" appears to lie outside the area that you've just identified as the Kosevo area.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, this is an entire plateau. This is an entire neighbourhood. I can't explain. Everything is in Kosevo, the hospital, the stadium. Everything is there. Everything is comprised within that name Kosevo. It's a wide plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right. Well then identify clearly the boundaries of the area that you consider to be the Kosevo area. You've just put a line there at the moment. Could you just identify clearly the area that you consider to be the Kosevo area.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, Kobilja Glava is somewhere around here. This would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right. Put the letter K next to that area.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now I'd like you to identify with a dot the location of the Jajce barracks. If I can remind you, we saw that it was just above a bend in the river which I think is fairly visible on this map.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, this is it. This is where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you see where the river is, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Now, could you put J next to the dot you've identified as the location of the Jajce barracks.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Now could you sign and date that, please. And you can sign it in the bottom right-hand corner, please, bottom right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5967, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, I think we can agree that when you were firing 120-millimetre mortar unit -- mortar round, I should say, from the Mrkovici area towards either the Kosevo area or the area of the Jajce barracks, that you were firing at an area where there is likely to be a substantial civilian population in that general area. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I accept that if we fired at the Jajce barracks. However, I told you that we were firing at the forward post of the Jajce barracks which was about a kilometre away from the location in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, in your statement, Mr. Gengo, at paragraph 18, you said: "Heavy weapons against our lines were mostly used from the firing positions from the sector of Kosevo below Grdonj and from the Jajce barracks." You did not there refer to the forward post of the Jajce barracks.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, that was also the Jajce barracks, and part of those barracks was the warehouse, Zmajevac, and that's how I responded when I was asked about the Jajce barracks. I explained that the location was not in the city but outside of the city. And all those were parts of the one and the same Jajce barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Nevertheless, we can accept or we can agree, I think, that when you were firing 120-millimetre mortar rounds from Mrkovici towards the locations that you've identified, the distance travelled by those projectiles would be of the range of 3 or 4 kilometres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I correct the transcript, please. In the previous answer it wasn't recorded that the witness said that he had already explained the issue of Zmajevac during the interview. That was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow. I leave it to you, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't able to understand the witness's answer. I'll move on anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you were approving the firing of 120-millimetre mortar rounds into the urban part of Sarajevo or towards the areas that you've identified in your evidence, what precautions did you take to minimise the possibility of civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: First of all, fire was never opened if it was not a response to enemy attack. When we were under attack, I used 120- and 80-millimetre mortars. I did not need to use them at any other time. So when we opened fire it was in response to the enemy fire that had been opened at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And I think you've said in your statement that positions of the Muslim unit opposed to you were in settlements which were continuously inhabited by civilians also. Now, when you were responding to fire --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: There were, Sedrenik settlement and some others, Vlasan Han [phoen] was also settled, the slopes of Grdonj were also inhabited. There were private houses there as well, family homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So as a general matter, what precautions did you take to minimise civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: What could I do for the enemy side? The enemy side should have done that. If they had opened fire from a settlement, they knew that we would respond. So they should have taken measures in order to avoid civilian casualties. I could not see whether there were any civilian people around that firing position or not. All I did was to return fire on the firing position from which fire had been opened on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is it your position that if the enemy side did not take measures in order to avoid civilian casualties, that that was their problem and you would fire anyway?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Of course, but of course. I could not see what they were doing at a distance of 3 to 4 kilometres. How was I in a position to see what they were doing over there?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to move now, please, to paragraph 27 of your statement. We're moving to sniping, Mr. Gengo. In paragraph 27 you said that the opposing forces had sniper rifles and passive scopes and they would fire at night. How did you know that the enemy's snipers were using passive scopes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I knew because on one occasion I had three casualties. Three of my men were killed after having been hit in the head and in the area of the eye. It is well-known that a sniper reacts to heat if they had IC devices and all of my men were hit in those areas, in the head and eye areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You also say: "They would fire against our positions and leave the area." How did you know that they left the area after firing against your positions during the night?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I knew because my men and men on the opposing side were neighbours and they communicated to each other and they would say to each other: Move away, we would use snipers. They were not happy because they knew that sniper fire would be returned by the opposing side and the location population was not happy and they were against those infiltrated units because before that it was peaceful, there were no fires, and fire -- fires opened, and they just disturbed the peace, they would just infiltrate briefly, they would kill, and then they would return.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a problem with the interpretation. It says here from lines 11 onwards, on line 13 it says that local Muslims would tell them: Move away, we will open fire. And the witness said that they informed the enemy, their neighbours, and they told them: Move away, some people have come and they will open fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you should be aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speak slowly when answering the question and I'll leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is it -- in your interview with me you told me that you found out that they would leave the area after firing against your positions after the war, that's when you found that out, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Of course. They talked to each other. After the war I talked to my people and I learned that that's how they had done things. They talked to each other during the war. They were neighbours. They exchanged opinions on various issues because they knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now I want to talk about the nature of the Serbian side's response. You said in your statement: "The Muslim local population regularly protested against their stays because they knew the Serbian side's response would follow." Can you clarify the nature of the Serbian side's response?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I can. For example, if they came closer to positions and if opened fire on the road, if there was a mortar on one of the vehicles, they would open fire. I had to neutralise such firing positions. I had to open fire. And as soon as you fire from a 120- or 82-millimetre mortar, you know that the target area is about 50 kilometres -- 50 metres -- 50 square metres wide. So there was a danger that there would be collateral damage and the civilian population protested.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not "kilometre."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Square metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So is it right you retaliated against sniper fire using mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: It depended on the area where it was, from where it opened fire. It dictated the use of response weapons. Sometimes it would be a mortar. Sometimes it was a 12.7 machine-gun. It all depended on the area from which it was fired from. That dictated your choice of a weapons that would be used to neutralise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please do not --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again there is a mistake in the interpretation. The witness said if the position was in the forest -- I apologise I have to ask the witness to slow down because very important. Things are being omitted from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We do not know how much we are missing. So could you repeat your answer from the part which said to the effect, "It all depended on the area from which it was fired from." Mr. Gengo, do you follow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you repeat your answer to the question whether it is right that you retaliated against sniper fire using mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If fire was opened from a forest, from a thick forest in Borije, then I had to use mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think we're noting a clear pattern by the accused of raising interpretation questions when he does not like the answer that the witness is giving. That's my personal observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's not go there. Could you take up the issue from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, I want to put to you a few words that you said in your interview with me when you were describing the nature of your response with mortar projectiles. You said that the mortar explodes and shrapnels have wider domain of causing injuries, so it was inevitable that the civilians would get hurt as well. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, before the witness answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get a reference for that? It would allow us to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, yes. It's in his interview which has the 65 ter number 24035.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But for the record, line 11, page 35, the "yes" was said by the witness, not by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, unless we want to bring up the witness's interview which the accused is free to do in re-direct, I propose to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I would like to now ask you a few questions, Mr. Gengo, about a location known as Spicasta Stijena. That -- you know this location?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The VRS held it throughout the 1992 to 1995 conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was there one evening, I believe, that it fell under ABiH control for one evening; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And what month or year was that in?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: In September. I believe that it was on the 18th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Of which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, apart from that evening it was under the control of the VRS throughout the conflict; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, from Spicasta Stijena you had an excellent view of that part of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Only the part known as Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: But it's certainly an excellent location to place, for example, a sniper unit if you wanted to strike people in Sedrenik, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Because my three trenches on Spicasta Stijena were under cross-fire from the enemy, from Kresa on the right and from Borovo on the left. They were always under cross-fire, and I had to dig those three trenches on Spicasta Stijena and I -- I can show you how the men who defended their part of the village approached those trenches. I could not have the snipers there. I did not have them. They were not trained, in any case. In any case, that part of Sedrenik is up to 1200 metres away and the difference in altitude is about 1600 metres -- 2600 metres. Spicasta Stijena is at 900 metres, Sedrenik is at 630 metres. It was impossible to open fire under those conditions. It would have been impossible even in peacetime, let alone under the conditions that we were in during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We agree that Spicasta Stijena does have an excellent view of Sedrenik, don't we?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes, there's a good view if it's not obstructed by someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your statement at paragraph 35, you said: "There were no trained sniper shooters in my battalion." Now, I want to talk about the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade. You worked at the command of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade from September 1992 until -- until January 1994?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You were in charge of technical supplies?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You worked under General Lizdek?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did the brigade have sniper weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes, as per establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: About how many sniper weapons did it have?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how many exactly, but it had M76 sniper rifles, JNA establishment rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We'll take this up after the break. Your Honour, we can take a break now if Your Honours wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we take a break, Mr. Gengo, I checked some evidence we have about the organisation of the SRK, and I noted there are two separate regiments with respect to artillery. One is the 4th MAP, which is called mixed artillery regiment; and the other seems to be 4th mixed anti-tank artillery regiment which was abbreviated as MPO --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An artillery regiment, not an anti-tank regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which was abbreviated as MPOAP. Does it ring a bell, Mr. Gengo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A mixed anti-armour regiment, a regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at five past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber needs to rise at the end of today at 2.30, so we asked around with the staff and thanks to the kind understanding we have decided to reduce the lunch break to half an hour today. So we'll take a break from 12.30 to 1.00. Yes, Mr. Robinson, I was told that you had something to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. You will recall that Dr. Karadzic asked for a reference from Mr. Gaynor to portions of the interview that the OTP had conducted with this witness and we never actually received the page reference but we did receive the 65 ter number. But in looking through that interview it raises some concerns that what Mr. Gaynor was putting to the witness is not accurately reflected -- reflecting what was said in the interview. And I point out, first of all, the question that Judge Baird came back to which is at page 17 of the transcript on lines 22 and 25, about whether or not Colonel Lizdek had to seek authority from anyone for approval. And on line 22, Mr. Gaynor said: "I suggest that you told me in our interview that only with the authorisation of General Galic first and later from General Milosevic could Lizdek approve the firing of a mortar round." And when going back to the actual interview on page 9 the question first was asked about through Colonel Lizdek you had to get authorisation and he said yes. And then: Who was his immediate superior? General Milosevic. And then Mr. Gaynor asked him: And Milosevic himself could order the use of a mortar. And the answer from Mr. Gengo was: "I don't know. I'm really not familiar with that line of duty." So we don't believe that Mr. Gaynor accurately put to the witness what he had said earlier. I have another point I want to make before I finish. And that is during the examination Mr. Gaynor suggested to the witness that he had not previously indicated in his statement that they were firing at the forward feature of the Jajce barracks, that he had only said in his statement that they were firing at the Jajce barracks. But in fact, on page 25 of the interview, Mr. Gengo informed Mr. Gaynor that -- he said that we were firing at the barracks Jajce, but that's forward feature, that's not the Jajce barracks itself. And we believe that it's improper for Mr. Gaynor to suggest to the witness that he had said something in the past that was inconsistent with his current testimony when Mr. Gaynor has in the very same interview information that the witness said something totally consistent with his testimony. So based on those two items we're concerned that the witness -- that things are being put to the witness unfairly, and we would like to have in the future references from Mr. Gaynor if he's going to refer to this interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I understood your first point, but I'm not sure about the second point you raised, Mr. Robinson. When Mr. Gaynor referred to Mr. Gengo's statement did he refer to the 92 ter statement or the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: He referred to the 92 ter statement, but yet -- knowing that the witness had said in the interview that they were firing at the forward positions. So I think as an advocate when you -- if you're trying to show that the witness has been mislead -- has been saying something inconsistent, if you have another more recent consistent statement, I don't think that it's proper to simply suggest that the witness is lying now because he said something different earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think Mr. Gaynor said Mr. Gengo was lying not talking about a forward position in his 92 ter statement, but let's move on. Yes, do you have any observation in response?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, two observations. I'm slightly concerned that Mr. Robinson has now mis-characterised the words of the interview. So we can either have the page in question of my interview with Mr. Gengo admitted in evidence or I can simply read out the relevant question and answer so that Your Honours have a full picture of that. I can simply read the questions and answers into the transcript right now if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or shall we --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Let's put that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Put questions to the witness when the witness is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. We can do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your -- another observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right, the second observation is this: My point was that the witness in his statement referred to Jajce barracks. He then showed up here, and in his interview with me he moved away from that and he said, Well, I was talking about the forward --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's not spend more time. I dealt with that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's bring in the witness. I overlapped again. What I said, Let's not go there -- I already forgot, but I said I dealt with it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps the Registrar -- thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps the Registrar could bring up 65 ter 24035, page 9, and we'll simply clarify the point with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm going to read to you a portion of an English language transcript of my interview with you, and I'd like to give you the opportunity to comment upon that if you have any comments to make. Now, on the page which is in front of the other participants in the courtroom at line 5 I said: "Okay. Take, for example, if you wanted to fire a mortar. Could you order the firing of the mortar? Or could the mortar crew order the firing of the mortar or did you have to go through Colonel Lizdek?" You responded: "Through Colonel Lizdek because," there's an unintelligible word then, "already the use of heavy weaponry and you had to get an authorisation from your respective superior command, because later you would have to justify the use of it." My question: "Okay. Now, was he authorised to approve the use of a mortar himself or did he have to get authorisation from another level?" Your response: "I understand, as far as I know, he would have to go in depth, meaning to ask from his superiors." Answer -- sorry, excuse me, my question: "And who was his immediate superior?" Your answer: "General Milosevic." My question: "And Milosevic himself could order the use of mortar?" Your answer: "I don't know. I'm not really familiar with that line of duty." Now, Mr. Witness, we clarified earlier that General Milosevic was the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: His predecessor was commander -- was General Galic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Would you like to make any clarifications whatsoever to the portion of the transcript that I've read out?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, it's not necessary. This is how things worked. This is how the chain of command functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could I ask, please, for P5945.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And we were talking about the question of sniper rifles within the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade. The document that's coming up is from General Lizdek of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade. It's dated the 29th of October, 1993, and I think we can see from it that Lizdek notes that his brigade has a total of 68 sniper rifles, 50 plus 14 plus 14. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes, that's probably correct. I didn't verify this, but yes, sniper rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And further down he says they had trained snipers from lower units. If we can go further down the English language, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I didn't -- I didn't have any such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In -- I accept your answer. In this document Lizdek says that they had trained snipers from lower units. Now, we also see that the sniper rifles in this document were 7.9-millimetre calibre and 7.62-millimetre calibre; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, were you involved in securing the delivery of large quantities of 7.62-millimetre rifles and ammunition from the VJ to the VRS in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, requests were certainly made to the technical and maintenance system. I can't remember what sort of requests. And then items were sent back. I can't remember the exact number, but this was an issue that was dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can we call up, please, P1279. This is a communication from General Dragomir Milosevic to the VRS Main Staff dated the 10th of July, 1995. Do you see in this document - perhaps it can be enlarged for you if necessary - that it seeks --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And it seeks the delivery of over 600, 7.62-millimetre rifles?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: They're clearly spelled out in the document itself. It also seeks the delivery of 378.000 bullets for 7.62-millimetre automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we can move down the English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Fine. I'll move on now to the Mostanica spring. You say in your statement at paragraph 29 -- sorry, just returning to that document, you do confirm, therefore, that you personally were involved in facilitating the supply from the VJ to the VRS of very large quantities of ammunition for 7.62-millimetre rifles; you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll turn now to paragraph 29 of your statement and there you refer to the Mostanica spring which you say was located in your battalion's zone of responsibility. Could we clarify whether you are referring to the Moscanica spring?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes, it's behind Moscanica and it is from there that part of the town of Sarajevo is supplied.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you say: "The VRS provided security for this water-supply line, made UNPROFOR's access possible, and that of the teams from Sarajevo in order to do checks and repairs and the water was never deliberately switched off." Now, that observation does not apply to the entirety of the conflict, does it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I was talking about the period during which the battalion was under my command, about the period during which this was my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you accept that the Serb side did, in fact, deliberately switch off water-supplies from the Moscanica spring during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I ask the Registrar, please, for 65 ter 1D02137.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Gengo, is only available in English so I will read to you the relevant paragraph. It's an UNPROFOR document dating from October 1993. If we can go, please, to page 3 in the English, and there are a number of paragraphs marked by asterisks at the second half of this document. And if we look at the bottom of the page, the penultimate paragraph says: "WHO experts suggest that the biggest humanitarian problem facing Sarajevo at the moment may be water. Recent shelling has cut the electricity to the Bacevo pumping station and has further disrupted the water distribution system. In addition, the Serbs have now cut off water coming from Moscanica, the small back-up system the city used to use when Bacevo was not functioning. The amount of available water in Sarajevo has consequently shrunk considerably. The incidence of Hepatitis A in the city is increasing. An epidemic is possible." Do you accept that on the basis of this document alone it appears that the Serb side did cut off water coming from Moscanica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. The water-supply wasn't cut off in my time. Things functioned normally. So I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to tender that document unless there's an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we do object. The witness hasn't confirmed anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I think we're back at the understanding I thought we had reached with the Defence where if the document sufficiently contradicts the witness's evidence, it is admissible on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, and I understand that, Mr. President, but since the witness indicated that during -- it wasn't during his time, then I don't think it directly contradicts and doesn't fall into this category.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well it's ... [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you have another opportunity to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now to orient everyone, the rest of the cross-examination will concern the Markale incident of the 5th of February, 1994. I want to start with the background to that incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, can I ask one question --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- to Mr. Gengo. I take it you've been staying in The Hague for a long time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was whether by any chance you followed the testimony of Mr. Dzida?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I can just clarify that he did have to return to Sarajevo. He just came in on Sunday night. He was here for the first week and not called and then he went back home, so he wasn't actually in The Hague during Mr. Dzida's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And from Sarajevo you didn't hear the testimony of Mr. Dzida?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Paragraph 33 which is on page 10 of your statement, you say: "There have never been plans to move our lines forward. It was the Muslims who kept attacking our positions. Their increased artillery activity had been notices since early 1994, usually followed by constant infantry attacks." Do I understand it that in the period the weeks preceding the 5th of February, 1994, there were no plans by the SRK to undertake offensive operations in the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: No, there were never such plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that there was no direction to your brigade in particular to undertake any offensive operations against the urban part of Sarajevo in the period before 5th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I call up, please, 65 ter 15575.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The document that's coming up, Mr. Gengo, is an order from General Galic dated the 26th of January, 1994. We can agree I think that this is about ten days before the shelling of the market-place; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could turn, please, to page 6 in English and page 4 of the original. At the end of section 2 there is a reference to: "Continue with offensive activities and liberate the Serb part of the city of Sarajevo." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to two -- well, first of all, can I ask you: Is that consistent with your assertion that there were no plans for any offensive operations at this time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: When it comes to my battalion, I never had such an order. There were never offensive activities planned. I was never involved in any such thing. My only duty and all I did was to defend my positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll take you to two other parts of this document. If we can go now, please, to page 8 in English which is page 6 in B/C/S. This part arises, I think, in a part of the document headed "decision of the commander." And if we look halfway down in English and in the third paragraph in the original, Mr. Gengo, it reads, I quote: "Further in the operation by holding the MOS in Sarajevo firmly encircled, inflicting casualties, preventing supplies from arriving, and preventing evacuations, using all means to exasperate them and with offensive activities along the following axes: Lukavica-Vojkovici-Hrasnica-Ilidza and Hadzici-Tarcin-Ivan Sedlo ..." and the order carries on. Now, that, I put it to you, is also inconsistent with your statement that there were no plans for any offensive actions.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
