utterances.text: In the area of responsibility of my battalion there were no such things and that transpires from this paragraph and I was not responsible for any other zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. Let's move -- you were at this time -- your battalion was in the 1st Rpbr, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And that is the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And you've confirmed earlier in your evidence that you had satisfactory communications from your battalion to that brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we turn now to page 9 in English and page 7 in B/C/S -- sorry, make that page 10 in English. I'm looking at the start of paragraph 5.2 which is halfway down in B/C/S and towards the top of the page in English. Now, the 1st Rpbr is the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You've already confirmed that your battalion was in that infantry brigade. I want to draw your attention to --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to five lines down in the English version and the fourth line in the B/C/S version, and in particular I'd like you to consider the words: "... put the Muslim forces under control in the urban part of Sarajevo ..." Do you see those words?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let the witness to read out the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you read out the first paragraph after -- in paragraph 5.2. Perhaps you can read it out loud, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, I understand this. I'm clearly on this. However, I did not participate in that. My only task was to hold my positions reached and that was it. There was nothing else to that on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: But do you accept that according to this document there was a plan ten days before the shelling of the market-place and that plan envisaged that your brigade should put the Muslim forces under control in the urban part of Sarajevo; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I did not have that document. I did not have this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I accept that you didn't have this order according to your evidence, but do you accept that is what is envisaged by this order?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I can read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5968, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, I'd like to turn now to the question of the mixed UNPROFOR/VRS commission, which you describe at paragraph 32 of your statement, and this - so everyone is aware - will take a fair portion of time. First of all, can you tell us when you first heard about the shelling of the market-place on the 5th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I heard the information on the radio that same evening, that a shell had fallen on the market-place, that there had been casualties. I heard it on Sarajevo radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you also see images on television?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I did too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Where were you when you saw those -- that footage on the television?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I was at the battalion command on Hresevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What station was it on, what television channel?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was your immediate reaction to the incident?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: It looked ugly, but I could tell that it had been staged.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You could tell by looking at the television footage that it had been staged; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, from what I could observe, the bodies, and some other details that could be seen in the market-place, I could conclude that everything had been prepared in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was Dzida at the battalion command with you while you were watching that broadcast?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you said in your statement that on the following day the mixed commission arrived, but you first heard -- let's go back to paragraph 32 at the start. You were informed on the 5th of February itself by the command of the 1st Romanija Motorised Brigade via the duty battalion that an inspection team would come to the zone of responsibility of your battalion. That was on the 5th of February, 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, when did you tell Dzida about the arrival of this inspection?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I told him immediately and I told him to be ready to go with them when they came. They arrived around 10.00 in two vehicles, one of them belonging to UNPROFOR, the other to the Main Staff, and I sent him to go with them, to take them where they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can we clarify, did you tell Dzida about the commission on the 5th or the 6th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I watched the TV on the 5th, and on the 6th the commission came around 10.00 on that same morning. On the 6th I told him to get ready to go with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you say in your statement that the commission requested a person from the battalion command who would take them to Mrkovici sector and the firing position of the 120-millimetre mortar which was suspected of being the weapon which fired the grenade at the Markale market. First of all, can we clarify as a matter of linguistics that the word you used for "grenade," do you mean --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I mean a shell, a grenade. It's all the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is it correct that the word you used refers to a mortar round, the word "grenata" in this context means mortar round; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes, of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you must have been deeply concerned when you heard the suggestion that a mortar unit under your command might have been responsible for what many believe to have been a massacre at the Markale market-place on the 5th of February?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. You must have been deeply concerned when you heard the suggestion that a mortar unit under your command might have been responsible for what many believe to have been a massacre at the Markale market-place on the 5th of February?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Of course. It was not like it was -- I was indifferent to it. But I know that it had not happened, so I was relieved in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You must have been determined to make it absolutely clear that no mortar unit acting under your command was involved in this incident?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility that it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: My question was about your frame of mind at the time. Can you confirm that you felt strongly that it should be shown that no mortar unit under your command was responsible for this incident?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Of course it was not involved. I was relieved because I knew that it hadn't been involved. I knew it then, I know it now, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So you knew even before the commission had set off that no mortar unit under your command was involved; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you name the members of the commission, first of all on the UNPROFOR side. Which UNPROFOR representatives arrived at your battalion headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I only know who the representative of the brigade was. He was always in charge of UNPROFOR. He was warrant officer Jakovljevic. I know that he was with them. He got out of the vehicle. He greeted me. Dzida got into the car. They went to the scene. They spent about three hours there, and Major Dzida briefed me. He gave me his feedback and that was that the commission had measured the distances, that it had established the -- controlling the mortars, that no fire had been opened from our positions. They had gone through all the motions. They had done whatever they had to do and that's what they established.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How many UNPROFOR representatives were in this commission?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. They were in the vehicle, they never got out of the vehicle, and I never counted them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene on the transcript. The witness said that they also uncovered the mortars, and that was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, it's your evidence that no member of this UNPROFOR team got out of the vehicle when they arrived at your battalion command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: The vehicles arrived and nobody got out of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You don't remember by any chance the nationality of any UNPROFOR member of this team?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: No, how should I remember them? They never got out of the car. I never saw them. I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And just for clarity, you don't know the first name nor the surname of any member of the UNPROFOR contingent?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: You mean of those who came on that day? I don't remember any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you name the members -- you've given us one name, Jakovljevic. Could you name the other members of this mixed commission on the VRS side.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Nobody but Jakovljevic got out. I saw him. I did not see -- I did not see any others. I didn't inspect their IDs. The commission had been set up by the Main Staff and it was not up to me to check who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You decided not to go with the commission yourself. You sent Dzida instead; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: He was always in charge of that part. Whenever the observers came, he would escort them to wherever they wanted to go. That was his regular duty. That was part of his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Lizdek didn't go with the commission either, did he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: No, just his representative went. I don't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, when the commission came back to you having conducted this inspection, what did Dzida tell you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: He told me that it had been established that no fire had been opened from our mortars, the mortars were there, they had never been moved, and everything was found to be in order there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This was extremely important information, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, of course, yes, it was. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No doubt you asked Dzida to put it in writing in a report addressed to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Of course he wrote a report, and that report was sent to the brigade command and I suppose that the brigade's representative drafted a report on his part.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you receive a copy of Dzida's report?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And did you keep it safely?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Together with the rest of the battalion documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, did you take steps yourself to make sure that the brigade command and indeed the corps command were fully aware of the outcome of this inspection?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Sir, there were representatives of a higher instance there and they were the ones who report to the brigade command, the corps command, the Main Staff. They were higher-ranking officers who were appointed to that commission, and it would have been out of order for me to teach them how to proceed on those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, apart from the report drafted by Dzida that you referred to, did Jakovljevic draft a separate report?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I suppose he did to the 1st Romanija Brigade, to those who had sent him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did anyone from this mixed commission provide you with photographs or videos or sketches of the scene; that is to say the location at Mrkovici where --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: No. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'll -- I'm going to bring up a series of documents and we're going to look for reference to this inspection on the 6th of February, 1994, and the documents will start on the 5th and then will go on. So I'd like to call up, please, 65 ter number 23901. This is a regular combat report to the SRK command of the 5th of February, 1994. The top of page 2 in English, please. And in the middle of -- sorry, at the bottom of page 1 in B/C/S we see the words: "First UNPROFOR reports on an alleged massacre are that the possible axis of attack was from the 1st Kosevo Infantry Brigade's direction." It straddles pages 1 and 2 in the English. Do you see that, Mr. Gengo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So first of all clarify one thing for the Court, please. According to this document, the allegation is that the attack was from the 1st Kosevo Infantry Brigade's direction. That's not your brigade, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: No. The Kosevo Battalion was down there under the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade, not the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of any inspection of mortars operated by the 1st Kosevo Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I don't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, this document -- take your time to inspect it if you like. But there's no reference to any intended visit by a mixed commission.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: On the 5th? What is the date of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document is the 5th of February. There's no reference in this. My point is this --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: The commission arrived on the 6th, not on the 5th, and in -- on the 6th, in the morning, I was informed that they would be arriving.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. But there's certainly no reference to any intended visit by a commission in this document, is there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: How could they have planned it if they didn't? I was only informed that they would be arriving and that I should provide somebody to escort them and it was the Main Staff and UNPROFOR who had planned that inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5969, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to call up, please, 65 ter 23884. This is an order from General Galic to all SRK units dated the 5th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is -- this document is a ban on fire against the urban part of Sarajevo according to its header, and I will -- you can see from the opening paragraph he says that: "Despite explicit orders, certain units, individuals, and artillery weapons crews have arbitrary and without approval been opening fire on urban parts of Sarajevo without need, instances of which have no effect." The paragraph after that he refers to the fact that Sarajevo was the focus of media and world attention and then he gives an order. And in that order he strictly forbids the opening of fire towards the urban part of Sarajevo without a special order of the corps commander except in the event of our positions being jeopardised and the lives of the combatants being threatened. Now, do you agree that this is an order to stop the offensive firing of weapons into the urban part of Sarajevo unless otherwise instructed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes. Orders frequently came instructing us to honour cease-fires, not to open fire. This was not the first order of that kind. It was constantly pressed upon us to respect cease-fires.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P5970.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to draw your attention briefly to two documents from Milovanovic in which he does raise the possibility of a Joint Commission. So can we please bring up D2182. This is an order from Milovanovic calling for the establishment of a Joint Commission. Now, in the third paragraph we're looking there at an UNMO translation. In the third paragraph down which is paragraph number 2, it says: "The work of the mixed expert artillery commission has to be documented (TV camera, photo shot, sketch, scheme, and so on) with all the necessary facts and figures." So I think there -- we can agree that there was an intention to establish a Joint Commission; isn't that right, Mr. Gengo?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the date for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First let's show the second page to the witness. This is a letter of General Milovanovic written in English to the UNPROFOR. And then shall we show the first page. On top of the page it is written that it is 5th of February and 3.30 on 6th -- 4.30, something to that effect. Yeah, date seems to be 5th of February, 4.30 in the afternoon. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So it seems from this document that Milovanovic did hold an intention to form a Joint Commission. Can we agree on that, Mr. Gengo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Based on this document I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why doesn't the witness have a Serbian version? Because in the text it says the 5th of January; however, it is clear that this was drafted on the 5th of February. It would be good for the witness to be provided with a Serbian version which is also the original of this document. There must be one in place. I'm sure there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you have, you can put it to the witness. Let's continue, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you've already confirmed, but I'd like you to re-confirm, that you never saw, Mr. Gengo, any television footage, any photos, sketches, or plans from the Joint Commission that you observed, did you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes, I never did. Only on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to call up, please, D2183.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we go further. Mr. Karadzic, it is you that tendered the previous document, and here you are asking for the B/C/S version. I think it's quite inappropriate intervention. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we uploaded the document in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no, I couldn't see it in B/C/S in the e-court. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, on the left we can see the B/C/S original. On the right is an English translation of this document which appears to have been created by UNPROFOR. Now, the part of this I want to draw your attention to, Mr. Gengo, is the part where General Milovanovic says that he has been informed that the Muslim side refuses to take part in the establishing and work of the joint military expert commission. And two paragraphs later, this is in the fourth paragraph: "Since the Muslim side is refusing to take part in the work of the mixed expert military commission, the headquarters of the Army of the Republic of Srpska is convinced that it has planned and instigated this dreadful massacre." And he goes on to deny any involvement or responsibility in what he describes as this evil crime. So I put it to you that this was, in fact, the end of the idea of General Milovanovic to form a Joint Commission. Well, before you answer that, let me draw your attention to one more part of it, Mr. Gengo. He says that: "The UNPROFOR command refuses that the Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR and the Chief of Staff of the so-called Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina together with," it continues on the next page in English, "the Chief of Staff of the Army of the Republic of Srpska go to the scene of the crime and uncover the consequences and the circumstances of this tragedy." I put it to you that when he says the "scene of crime" there he's talking about the suspected origin of fire in VRS territory. So again I put it to you, Mr. Gengo, that this was the end of General Milovanovic's idea of a Joint Commission.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where can we find this? Where is this written?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I've just read from the last paragraph of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what it is you would like me to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please hold on, everybody. Please slow down on your part as well. And please do not overlap while the interpretation is going on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I intervene now? Where does it say what Milovanovic means by the "scene of the crime"? And how can this refer to the location where shots were fired from, where shells were fired from, when the location in question is Markale?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- let -- let's go back. So you read out the passage. Could you put your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We'll leave the scene of the crime for a moment, Mr. Gengo. But do you agree that from this document it appears that General Milovanovic's idea of a Joint Commission came to a premature end and there was no Joint Commission?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say. I'm not familiar with what happened. All I know is that the commission came to see me, but as to who organised it, it wasn't for me to give much thought to such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. And I would like to put it to you that where General Milovanovic refers to a visit by the ABiH, the VRS, and UNPROFOR to the scene of the crime, he is - in the context of this letter - referring to the origin of fire. I put that interpretation to you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I don't know what was at stake, what requests they had made. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to the 6th of February, 1994, and we'll call up, please, 1D01655. This, Mr. Gengo, is a regular combat report, reporting the situation at 1600 hours on the 6th of February, 1994. The report is to the SRK command. Now, in paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's written by the SRK.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're -- just after this we're about to come to a document which appears to go from the SRK command to the VRS Main Staff. It's my understanding that this particular document is a document preceding that later document which is to the SRK command. But I'm quite happy for that to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's signed by General Milosevic, wasn't it? Very well. Let's continue. I leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I would like to make sure I'm showing Your Honours the correct document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can see the list. Can we see the page 2, both versions, on the e-court. Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. This is, indeed, signed by General Milosevic. I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I think we see at paragraph 3 of this document if we could go to -- first of all, on this page at least, Mr. Witness, there is no reference to a visit of a Joint Commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we can go to the preceding page, please. Now, in this document, as the Presiding Judge has correctly pointed out, it is from General Milosevic. Again, there is no reference to a visit of a Joint Commission; although, it does at paragraph 3 refer to a meeting on events in Sarajevo which was held in the corps command attended by President Karadzic, General Gvero, UNPROFOR, and UN representatives.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So you agree that there's no reference in this document anywhere to this visit of the Joint Commission that you've given evidence about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5971 , Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to call up now, please, 65 ter 24034.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document is to the VRS Main Staff from the SRK command dated the 6th of February, 1994, and it's a regular combat report with the situation at 1800 hours. Once again -- well, first of all, we can observe that this replicates much of the information that we saw in the earlier report. Again in paragraph 3 we see the reference to a meeting held at the corps command attended by President Radovan Karadzic, Major-General Gvero, and UNPROFOR and UN representatives. What we do not see, Mr. Gengo, is any reference whatsoever to the mixed commission visit which you said took place earlier on the day of this document.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: The commission paid a visit. I don't know whose orders they were following. This is something I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: But do you accept that this document does not refer to that visit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: It doesn't refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5972, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to call up, please, now 1D01656.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We're moving now to the 8th of February, 1994. This is a regular combat report dealing with the position at 1600 hours on the 8th of February, and there's no reference in this to a mixed commission either. Take your time to read it, Mr. Gengo, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So you agree there is no reference to that mixed commission, is there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5973, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Gengo, we'll move on a week now to the 14th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I call up, please, D2378.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is a document from Colonel Radislav Cvetkovic to the SRK command and to the VRS Main Staff. He says in the opening paragraph of this document - if we can go down a little further in the English, please - that he was appointed to an international committee on the 14th of February -- excuse me, correction, on the 13th of February, 1994. Now, that's eight days after the purported visit on the 6th of February, 1994, isn't it, Mr. Gengo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if we have a look at page 3 in the English we see that he says -- well, first of all, if we can go up a little on the English version. Well, he says in this document that as a representative of the VRS he was asked by the members of the commission for technical information proving that the Serbian side did not launch the shell. Do you see that reference?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not very clear. Could we zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you see it better now?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, does it not strike you as strange that he would say that if it was eight days after you claim that an international commission had already inspected the mortar units at Mrkovici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact dates. I know this event occurred, but I don't know when exactly. I did not keep any written records. But I know that the commission paid a visit; however, I do not remember Cvetkovic paying a visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we can look at the next page in English, please. And here - that's the next page in B/C/S as well, please - Cvetkovic says: "I strongly denied the possibility that a shell was launched from the Serbian side and offered the commission to visit the suspected place ..." Again, that statement by Cvetkovic is totally inconsistent, is it not, with the fact that the VRS had already brought an international commission to visit the suspected place eight days earlier?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: The commission paid a visit, but I cannot remember the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We'll move on, please, to P1441, please. Now, this next document is in the English language, Mr. Witness, so I'll tell you briefly what it is. It's a compilation of several different documents, most -- the bulk of this is -- are documents produced by UNPROFOR in the days following the Markale I massacre. And I've gone through the entirety of this bundle of documents, Mr. Gengo. There's not a single reference to the mixed commission visit of 6th of February, 1994. And I'm going to bring you to three pages of it which I will put to you in due course strongly suggests that that visit never took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to page 41. This is a part of annex D.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And this portion of this bundle of documents, Mr. Witness, there is a summary of the evidence of ten UNPROFOR officers and other personnel who were involved in investigations relating to the Markale massacre or the Markale incident, if you prefer, on the 5th of February, 1994. Not one of those summaries refers to a visit to Mrkovici on the 6th of February or any kind of visit to SRK positions. And on this page we see a reference to Colonel Pardon - under number 9 if we can go down a little - he refers there to an inspection which he attended to mortar positions held by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He says from there they visited a 120-millimetre mortar position in Kosevo stadium where they saw a 120-millimetre mortar. He then gives its unit, which is M75, number 2977, I should say the mortar unit's number. And he refers later to a visit to a second position, again of a mortar unit controlled by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There's no reference to any visit to mortar units controlled by the Bosnian Serbs. If we can go now, please, to page 44 which is part of Annex E. This document, Mr. Gengo -- if we can perhaps go to the next page of this, please. Yes, sorry, to the previous page at the bottom under paragraph 4, please. Just below paragraph 4. I'll read out the relevant part of it to you, Mr. Gengo. It says: "Colonel Cvetkovic, CO, BSA Artillery Regiment stated that Kosevo Brigade has mortar positions (including 120-millimetre mortar) in the Mrkovici area (BP 9463). These positions have not been visited by UN personnel in at least four months, and cannot be located with any accuracy. Since October 1993, UNMOs have been denied freedom of movement in this brigade area, although most shots fired from the area can be observed from UNMOs in adjacent areas." And finally I'll take you to a third reference in this document, that is in Annex G at page 56. This page, Mr. Gengo, refers to a meeting held on the 13th of February, 1994, in Pale between some UNPROFOR representatives and Colonel Cvetkovic. In the second paragraph it says that Colonel Cvetkovic confirmed that he was to act as the Bosnian Serb representative for purposes of the UN investigation into the Sarajevo market explosion of 5th of February, 1994. Now, if we go down to the fourth paragraph it says: "Colonel Cvetkovic then discussed numerous aspects of the incident in theoretical terms, and offered his personal opinion concerning the validity of events as portrayed by the media. He had no specific evidence to offer of direct relevance to the investigation." Now, Mr. Gengo, I think we can agree that the results of an inspection of 120-millimetre mortar positions which might have been held on the 6th of February, 1994, would be of direct relevance to the investigation, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: That concerns my area of responsibility, my mortars. As for the Kosevo mortars, I don't know, I didn't go there, but they continually visited my area and I co-operated with the UNPROFOR representatives who kept visiting my area and they would sometimes announce their visits and sometimes they would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And do you not find it strange that Colonel Cvetkovic makes no mention whatsoever, according to this note, of the meeting of the inspection of the 6th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't Cvetkovic who was in charge of the mortars. He was the commander of a mixed artillery regiment. He had his guns in that area of responsibility. He did not have any mortars there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Are you seriously suggesting that Colonel Cvetkovic would not have been aware of an inspection which had been carried out on the 6th of February, 1994, between members of the VRS Main Staff and others with UNPROFOR officials?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about Cvetkovic, whether the Main Staff organised that commission. I don't know whether and how they organised it and according to whose orders. I just went to the site, that's all I know. I'm not aware of anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Finally we'll show a brief video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 45200. According to the clip, it appears to date from the 10th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: "I can't answer your questions. I just want to say that we are not going -- we don't have any reason to go on with the conference until we get an international investigatory body to investigate and resolve the Sarajevo massacre. I would remind you that Muslims have staged -- managed the killing in bread queue killing 18 of their own people, and Yugoslavia got sanctions. Then Muslims have shut down the Italian air traffic and Serbs got no-fly zone resolution. Now, until this massacre, Serb side getting an ultimatum -- an ultimatum from NATO. We don't have any reason to go on with the conference until we get commission to investigate every single circumstance and to say publicly who is the responsible for this massacre. "We are going to pose that and to demand an international investigatory body to get findings and to make it public."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in that -- first of all, for the record, we can agree that that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We agree, Mr. Gengo, that was President Radovan Karadzic speaking there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in that clip, Radovan Karadzic is calling for an international investigatory body to get findings; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And he makes several other references which are along the lines of the need to get an international commission to look into this incident; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And he makes no reference whatsoever to any mixed VRS/UNPROFOR commission that might already have been formed in this clip?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Every incident that happened on the line caused representatives of UNPROFOR and representatives of the brigade to came -- to come to the scene, and that was the case in every incident that happened in the zone of responsibility. Controls were stepped-up as soon as something happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that clip, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5974, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note that it's just beyond 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much longer would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Probably about three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then shall we continue --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- and conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I'd like to bring up an order from President Karadzic dated the 7th of February. That's P846, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: As you can see, Mr. Witness, this document bears the stamp of the Presidency of the Republika Srpska, I believe, as well as the signature of Dr. Karadzic. In paragraph -- in the first paragraph we see that Karadzic is saying: "There is evidence that Serbs are not responding in equal measure to Muslim artillery provocations - sometimes 20 to 30 or even 70 times more." Now, I put it to you, Witness, that that statement by President Karadzic is not consistent with your assertion in paragraph 33 of your statement that it was the Muslims who kept attacking your positions and to your position that SRK forces were firing back only when fired upon in equal measure?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: That's correct. In 1994 and 1995 -- lacked ammunition. The Muslims had more and that's why they shelled us more. We had to be economical with our ammunition because we did not have enough. Our supplies had been depleted. That's why we did not respond in equal measure to the fire opened by the opposing side. We didn't have enough ammunition. At least that was the case in the zone of responsibility of my battalion. I don't know about the others. Ammunition was expensive, difficult to get by, and when -- we had to account for every single round, every single bullet, let alone a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Gengo, you're aware that the president of the republic was receiving constant supply of information from the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, then why would the president refer to in this document to retaliation by the Serb side 70 times greater to incoming fire received from the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. That's calling for speculation on behalf of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No -- let's put it differently. Witness answered that the Serbs were retaliating or responding less than what they were shelled. Could you read out the first paragraph, Mr. Gengo. Could you read aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "There is evidence to the effect that the Serbian side responds inadequately to the Muslim fire, sometimes even 20 to 30 times more." I don't know what this means. I'm really not clear. This is absolutely impossible. We didn't have the necessary ammunition. We could not do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll wrap-up now, Mr. Witness. I've shown to you today a series of documents from -- which contain records of what was said by Colonel Cvetkovic, by the SRK command, by UNPROFOR, by the president of the republic about this extremely serious incident. Not one of them refers to an inspection of the 120-millimetre mortar guns at Mrkovici on the 6th of February, 1994. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And I further put it to you that this commission, insofar as it did exist -- correction. I'll start again. I'll put it to you, Mr. Gengo, that this commission did not exist; and if it did, that it was essentially a sham.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I don't know if it was a sham or not. I only know that a commission did arrive. There were two vehicles. I don't know on what -- on whose orders. The brigade command informed me that they would arrive. I followed the orders and everything else was up to them. It was their concern, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's it for me. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gengo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm very satisfied with the fact that the Prosecution does more than they can. They shouldn't do more than they ought to. The questions have been so confusing and so misleading on the witness that I should be given quite a lot of time to put my additional questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I asked it because of the -- only for the purpose of scheduling matter. We'll take a break then for half an hour and resume at ten past. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Colonel, sir, earlier today on page 31, lines 16 through 21, you were asked whether you had controlled and how you made sure that the number of collateral casualties was reduced. I'm going to read to you what you said during your interview with the Prosecutor. I would like to call up 65 ter 24035, which is the transcript of that interview. It is on page 3539. We have it, yes, 3539. I apologise, page 11, 32 -- page 11, line 32. You were asked and I'm going to read in English. It will be interpreted much better than the other way around. [In English] "Okay. So if you didn't know what was around their fire points, how could you be sure that you weren't firing in the area where there might be civilian targets?" [Interpretation] Your answer was as follows: [In English] "I couldn't be sure of that. I didn't know who was there. So, the one who is firing from the other side should have thought of the civilians over there. Because if it had been from my side, I would done it in such a way." [Interpretation] My question to you is this: This assumption of yours, is it based on the fact that on the other side and there were officers who had been through the same schools as you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's leading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well very well then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you then tell us based on which did you assume that they would have done the same thing you would have done in terms of the protection of civilians?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I assume that they knew that when a shell hit shrapnel dispersed for about 50 metres around. And if they did not secure the civilians, some of the civilians that found themselves in the area of fire may have been harmed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have page 13 in the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 18 of today's transcript, lines 9 and 10, you were asked whether you effectively exercised control over the battalion and whether you were sure that mortars were not fired without your approval. And now I'm going to remind you of your answer given to the Prosecutor during the interview on line 10. The question was as follows: [In English] "Was anyone in your battalion ever detained for firing a projectile into the city of Sarajevo?" [Interpretation] Answer: [In English] "In my time, during my time there was no such lack of discipline." [Interpretation] Question: [In English] "No, my question was: Was anyone in your battalion ever detained for firing the projectile into the city of Sarajevo?" [Interpretation] Answer: [In English] [As read] "No. There was offence of that kind during my time. If I had been -- if it had been, then he would have been detained for sure." [Interpretation] Do you still stand by that position?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt for a moment. The transcript as far as the Prosecution is concerned at line 18 of page 13 that Mr. Karadzic is reading from where it says "There was offence of that kind" it's our position that that inaccurately omits the word "no." The transcript should read: "There was no offence of that kind." I'm simply saying that so that the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you to tell us where was the forward command post Butile in respect of the zone of responsibility of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Butile? It's on a completely different side, in the Rajlovac and Ilidza sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you about that visit. Those who visited you, were they the same people who were members of the investigation commission?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: People visited me all the time. I can't tell you how many times a week, but they were always there. Whenever an incident occurred, they came to inspect and to see what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So do you know that the investigation commission was set up after the 6th and do you make a distinction between --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Objection. Once again, despite repeated instruction from the Trial Chamber, Dr. Karadzic is using leading questions in re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies. I really admit that my habits from cross-examination die hard. I'll have to educate myself not to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, let me ask you this: Do you make a distinction between an ad hoc inspection and a permanent investigation commission?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I don't make any distinction. I didn't make any distinctions. They came. They were in the vehicles. I don't know who they were. I don't know when the commission was set up -- when it was supposed to be set up. I really don't know. Commissions were always there. They came frequently. I didn't get involved in any of the conversations with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can I now call up 65 ter 15575. Now it has a different number because it has been admitted into evidence. Can we see it in e-court, please. You were asked, Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, about the tactics applied by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and with the help of this document Mr. Gaynor wanted to obtain a confirmation that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had offensive intentions and offensive activities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at bullet point A where it says "tasks of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps." Are these offensive or defensive measures?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Defensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I please ask you to read the first sentence in the following paragraph. Could you please read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: My vision is not that good. Can you do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "By construct a grouping of the troops and with an appropriate reinforcement with the reserve forces of the Main Staff of the VRS, improve the operations, the tactical position, the Sarajevo sector." Can you please tell us whether Zuc, Hum, and Mojmilo are areas settled by Muslims or are these some other kind of features?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Zuc was inhabited by Serbs. They came under attack by Muslim forces and then I would say that it was an elevation that was almost empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the following paragraph it says [indiscernible] the Muslim forces and capture the Hranjen and Podhranjen features. What are these?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: This is wasteland. There was nobody there. Those were points held by the Army of Republika Srpska and they wanted to link-up those two areas because the line went --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Have you finished your answer, Mr. Gengo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic didn't read out the sentence in full, the first sentence. After that it continues to read like this, after saying, "Improve the operations tactical positions in the region of Sarajevo," the sentence goes on like this: "Penetrate to the left bank of Misoca river, liberate the villages of Zabrdje, Sokolje, Zuc, Hum, and Mojmilo." Then I'd like to ask you what does this liberation mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this a question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means to improve the tactical position, to move one part of the line in order to conquer it, to take that area, to improve one's defence position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You told us just now that it means to take that area? So that's an offensive -- for the purpose of defence --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To improve one's positions. This is the improvement of one's positions, not taking a town but improving one's positions to improve one's defence abilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So liberating what, Mr. Gengo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One part of the line, one part of the tactical position. In -- and this was carried out in the sectors from which we were threatened. We had to liberate -- actually to -- we had to prevent a situation where our population may have been threatened from those --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is a lot of background noise in the courtroom so the interpreter could not hear the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did you say? Your population may have been threatened from where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the elevations that were occupied by them, the population and the road were threatened. From there and in order to improve that part of the position for our forces had to take those positions in order to prevent the threat to our population in Vogosca, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, so can you tell the Trial Chamber where the Misoca river is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: The Misoca river is in Ilijas. That used to be a military warehouse in the past and it stored technical fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There is a reference here to the liberation of Zabrdje which is described as a village. Do you know who resided there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Serbs did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that a village where the president of the Assembly, Krajisnik, was born?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the other features, Sokolje, Zuc, Mojmilo, Orahovica, Hranjen, Podhranjen? Were those Muslim settlements or something else?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: There was nobody there. It was a wasteland. Podhranjen was not settled. It is a place in the direction of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at bullet point 4. Usually it is a decision by the commander. Let me read it to you: "I decided by engaging the main body of the corps in the decisive defence, prevent the link up of the enemy forces from the Muslim part of Sarajevo with the forces attacking along the valleys of the Neretva river, Zujevina [phoen] river and the Bosnia river along the following axis, Olovo, and so on, to stabilise the front line and fully fortify the positions thus creating secure support points for the defence of the Pretis, Orao, Famos industrial facilities and the TRZ and safely hold the MOS in Sarajevo encircled." Can you tell the Chamber how you understand this decision? Is this a decision for defensive or offensive activities?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Defensive because it was not aimed at conquering Sarajevo but preserving what we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go to page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the first sentence. I'll read it out. It says: "The focus of the attack should be in the Grbavica sector. The Zeljeznica stadium and Sanac [phoen]." It says carry out fortification work and so on and so forth. Is this defensive or offensive action?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Defensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's see 5.2 now, it's been read out to you: "The 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade defends its positions in the zone of responsibility through a persistent and decisive defence, and in co-operation with the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade and the Vogosca Tactical Group in active combat, smash enemy forces in the region of Colina Kapa-Ophodza-Orlovac and Grdonj and improve the tactical position of the brigade. Put the Muslim forces under control in the urban part of Sarajevo while constructing heavy fortification and setting up the full-on obstructions in front of the forward line of defence using the system of fire to prevent the enemy penetration into the defence zone." Is this offensive or defensive action with fortifications and with tactical improvements?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: This is defensive measure taken to improve the tactical position of our units in the area of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Chamber what these features are where your brigade is supposed to rout the enemy, Colina Kapa, Orlovac, and Grdonj?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, these were deserted areas, hills. There was no one there. There were hills that posed a threat to our positions, to our roads. So there were no features of any significance so there -- there's footage of the area and this can be seen in the footage, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When asked by Mr. Gaynor represented -- attorney from the Prosecution you said you didn't participate in this and you didn't know. Now how do you know that this was defensive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know these positions. I observed these things when they took place, but my unit did not take part in the events, in the operations. But I was aware of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apology. You didn't say you didn't know. I'm reading that transcript again. Very well. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, sir, is it clear, it says improve the tactical positions and carry out fortification work. Someone with offensive operations, does such a person engage in improving fortifications or is this defensive?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Well, if you want to mount a defence you carry out fortification work. If you want to carry out an attack then you break through and try to conquer areas. We never received such an order to go on Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did we consider Sedrenik, Stari Grad, Bascarsija Serbian parts of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: No, there were not many of our inhabitants down there. Mostly there were Muslims in Bascarsija, Sedrenik, and in other parts. There were some of our people who lived down there from Vucije Luke [phoen]. They had houses in Sedrenik. So that was their area, in fact. Ninety-nine per cent of the area was inhabited by their people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when it says liberate Serbian parts of town, does this refer to the core part of the town, the inner town in which the inhabitants are mostly Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to conclude with this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue. That was leading, though.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The SRK and your brigade, where were they in contact with the enemy and were there two types of front lines?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes. They were in contact with them in the area of Gorazde towards the 81st Division and also in the direction of Sarajevo where there was the 105th and the 110th Brigades, I think, facing us, also in the outer ring in the Nisici area they were in contact with the 3rd Corps and the 2nd Tuzla Corps. We were in contact with them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at page 6 very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the top it says regroup the forces of the corps and carry out with the Drina Corps an action, take control of the Zvijezda mountain, liberate the route in Srednje Olovo, route the enemy in the Cemerska mountain sector, and so on and so forth. Could you tell us where these places are located? Was there a difference when it comes to tactics of the SRK deployed against the external ring and deployed against the internal ring?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: This position is to the north above Ilijas and towards the Nisici plateau. That's where the road led to Sokolac. That part was defended so that the 1st Corps units and the 2nd and 3rd Corps units didn't link up so that the inhabitants in Ilijas, Hadzici, Ilidza, Vogosca, and Rajlovac would remain encircled. So we had to defend this position so that the Muslim forces would not link up and they wouldn't cut off part of the town inhabited by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at page 14, please, 6, item 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll read out the sentence: "Logistic support of prisoners of war is to be provided in accordance with the Geneva Conventions." Were you aware of the fact that this was the corps commander's position?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, I'm just noticing another couple of leading questions are infecting the re-direct again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I took it that -- just the witness confirmed that it's written there. Let us continue. Let's conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have a look at P5969 very briefly, page 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 58 -- on page 58 of today's transcript you were shown this document and I would like to ask you about something that concerns Mrkovici. Does it say that fire was opened from Mrkovici or that fire was opened by them on Mrkovici? Let's have a look at it at the beginning. "The enemy: "Infantry and sniper fire attacks in the sector of Hresa, Faletici, Mrkovici, Azici, Nedzarici," et cetera. This is the enemy taking action, and number 2, it says: "Our forces: "Fire was opened in response on observed enemy targets in the area of the Vogosca Tactical Group, 120-millimetre mortar and 40-millimetre PAT anti-aircraft gun were used." So does it say that fire was opened from Mrkovici or that that was not the case? Where did you retaliate from?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: 120-millimetre? No, I didn't have any such thing. From Mrkovici, I can't really see where was opened from. If fire was opened on Hresa, on Mrkovici, well, then I retaliated. But as for Vogosca, if it was Vogosca, then they retaliated probably because I couldn't do anything in Vogosca with a 120-millimetre mortar and a 40-millimetre PAT. I didn't have any such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fire was opened from infantry and artillery from Mrkovici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Sometimes they fired from tanks from the Ciglane area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, today -- on the 5th of February, what did they use to fire on Mrkovici and was there any retaliation, any response from Mrkovici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: No, not on the 5th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you asked about measures to reduce collateral casualties, when using mortars, heavy-calibre weapons, did you have the duty of observing fire that was opened?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: If you could see where the hits landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now for my last question. After everything you heard, given all the questions put to you and the documents you have seen, could you tell us whether the Army of Republika Srpska fired a shell on Markale on the 5th of February, 1994, from the area under your control?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: I can claim with full responsibility that the VRS did not fire a shell on the Markale Market.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, this is not very important, but I'll put to you, Mr. Gengo -- shall we upload the Exhibit P5968, 65 ter 15575, English page 8. I remember B/C/S page was 6, if my memory was correct. The middle of big paragraph it reads like this: "And by using all available means exert strong pressure on the Muslim forces in Sarajevo and liberate Debelo Brdo, Mojmilo, Colina Kapa, Grdonj, Hum, Golo Brdo, Zuc, Vis, Mijatovica, Kosa, Sokolje and Stupsko Brdo and penetrate deep into the region of Brekin [phoen] Potok and Dobrinja ...," and then it reads like this: " ... creating thus favourable conditions for the wider-scale offensive activities by the forces of the corps and the reinforcement." So my question for you, Mr. Gengo, is: What does this wider-scale offensive activities mean?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: It means wider activities on the positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What activities?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Combat activities, improving the tactical position. In order to move a line to fortify you have to get the enemy to move from a hill in order to take it, in order to have a dominant position. So you had to do this in order to dominate given part of town because when Muslim forces attacked it was necessary to be able to mount a defence and prevent the external ring from being penetrated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, does General Galic not say "offensive activities"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Could I have a look at that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I can't find the location in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a hard copy. It's the first paragraph in the B/C/S version and we do have a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "... creating thus favourable conditions for the wider-scale offensive activities ..." Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what General Galic had in mind, but I know what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Unless --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just put another question to the witness on the basis of your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary. The witness answered to the far --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be useful for the Chamber. Perhaps you could ask the witness whether any of these hills were taken by the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not necessary, Mr. Karadzic. Unless my colleagues have questions for you, Mr. Gengo, that concludes were you evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And who is the next witness, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Stojan Dzino.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's bring in the next witness. While we are waiting, Mr. Robinson, with respect to the accused's motion for extension of word limit for request for review of Registrar's decision on indigence, where the Defence requests an extension from 3.000 to 5.000 words to challenge the Registry's decision of 11th of October, 2012, on Mr. Karadzic's indigency, we will hereby grant this request and order that his request for review of the Registry's decision of 11th of October not exceed 5.000 words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Take a seat and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Dzino.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D1605 in the e-court system, please. 6085, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, while we're waiting for that to appear, what rank did you have when you left the army?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: I had the rank of lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you give the Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to remind you and remind myself that we should speak slowly and pause between question and answer because the interpreters might leave something important out, not through any fault of their own but because of us. Is this a statement that you gave, the one on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this statement accurately reflect the questions -- the answers you provided to the questions put to you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant, if I were to put the same questions to you today, would the substance of your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender this statement into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No objection to the statement. There's no associated exhibits I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2387, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, as you noted, your evidence in chief was admitted in the form of writing, i.e., your statement, in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be further cross-examined by the Prosecution. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I be allowed to read out a brief summary, just one page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I forgot that. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll read it out in English. [In English] Stojan Dzino did his military service as a soldier in 1992. Between March and May 1992, he was on guard duty in the village of Bojnik, Rajlovac. In December 1992, he was a battalion commander in the vicinity of Sarajevo. At the beginning of 1994, when the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade was established he was appointed assistant commander for morale in the 4th Infantry Battalion. As early as in 1991, Stojan Dzino already heard of the arming of Muslims and the membership of many to the Patriotic League and the Green Berets. In the summer and autumn 1991 it was noted that the SDA leaders frequently visited Ahatovici. The situation at that time was already tense. In March 1992, after the murder of a Serbian wedding guest in Bascarsija night guards started begin organised in the different settlements by the local population. These guards were operational until the 29th of May, 1992. By initiative of some Serbs, meetings were held in the local community in the period from March to May 1992 to discuss the possibility of restoring trust and peace in the settlements. The last meeting took place at the end of May 1992, when Hasan Nujkic and two other men all dressed in camouflage uniforms and wearing green berets called on all the Muslims to leave the gathering, and they proceeded to do so. After this last failed attempts to peaceful -- to a peaceful solution, the first Muslim offensive was launched on the 29th of May, 1992, against Krstac locality. Stojan Dzino and approximately ten men set out to Krstac where they engaged the Muslims who retreated in the direction of Gornje Mioce and his men took control of the ridge and held it until the end of clashes. On June the 2nd, 1992, another confrontation took place in which several Muslims were captured and others killed. Stojan Dzino knew every family in the area and he only recognised a negligible number of the captured and killed Muslims. All the wounded captured Muslims were given first aid and there was no maltreatment. In the zone of combat operations in which he was, there were no dishonourable activities, rapes, slaughters, maltreatment, et cetera. With regards to the Butile barracks, the area in front of the barracks was laid with mines towards the Serbian village of Osijek, whereas towards Pasici and Bojnik there were no mines but a fence, but the wire was broken in places so that there were various paths. Those villages are Muslim. Stojan Dzino has knowledge that the 1st Corps of the Army of BH was under control of the Muslim authorities in the period from April 1992 to December 1995. The 1st Corps held positions in civilian zones. His unit and the other units towards the city of Sarajevo as well as on the outer ring had only defence tasks. The complete zone was in an unfavourable position in relation to the enemy side. The distance between the lines of separation ranged between 9 metres and to the closest -- at the closest point and 100 metres at the greatest distance.
