During all four years of the war, there were negligible movements of the line to his unit's detriment. Fire was never opened in the depth of territory against civilian facilities. Neither he nor his unit, nor lower or superior commands, ever harboured any intention to cause civilian casualties or terrorise civilians in the area and under Muslim control, nor exert psychological -- or exert psychological influence on them. His unit never received any oral or written order from higher command or civilian authorities to carry out attacks against civilians or means of public transportation in the territory under Muslim control, nor did he ever issue such order. In the zone of responsibility of his brigade and as far as he is aware, beyond it there were no paramilitary units. All independent units were included in the command and control of the respective brigades. There were very few members of his unit who were professional servicemen, and those who were had been born in the area. The rest were mostly local men and the commanding officers were mostly from the reserve. His unit hardly volunteered into its ranks. Stojan Dzino categorically states that in four years of warfare he never saw a professional sniper in his unit or other units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. On the contrary, they had intelligence that snipers in the unit of 1st Corps of BH army were targeting civilians in the part of the town under the control of Serbian authorities as well as those in the town under Muslim control. Muslim forces also cut off water-supply to his unit's zone of responsibility and re-supplied their units using humanitarian aid convoys. Muslim forces would also frequently violate cease-fire agreements. His unit co-operated extremely well with the municipal civilian authorities. In Rajlovac there were no persecution policy based on religious or ethnic ground. [Interpretation] At this point in time I don't have any questions for the Lieutenant and I hand him over to the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I -- as I informed you, you'll be examined -- cross-examined by Mr. Gaynor. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dzino. I'm here to ask you a few questions on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: First of all, in 1990 you were a resident in the municipality of Novi Grad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Specifically Mihaljevici?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Serb Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you stand for election -- in elections taken in 1990?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You were not a candidate for the Serb Democratic Party in any elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I call-up, please, 65 ter number 24029. This document does not have an English translation at present, Mr. President. We'll see in a moment that it is fairly self-explanatory. We will get an English translation uploaded as soon as we can. I think if you go halfway down or it can stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We can see that this is a list of candidates for the Municipal Assembly of Novi Grad in Sarajevo. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Under the second list of candidates we see a list of candidates for the Serb Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Let's focus in on the name which is number 78 on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on that, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Number 78 lists Dzino Stojan, a Serb from Mihaljevici; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: This is not correct. Listen, this is a list. As a matter of fact, I would like to know the date when this list was compiled or, rather, when this was published in a newspaper. This must be a newspaper or a magazine, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The date at the top of the page is the 16th of November, 1990.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Listen, in order for the Serbian Democratic Party to run in Novi Grad municipality, the Serbian Democratic Party -- not us on the list. A hundred people had to be put forth in Novi Grad municipality, present their IDs, and say that they are members because it would give the Serbian Democratic Party the right to run in the elections. This is not a list of candidates. This is a list of the 100 people who put their names towards helping the Serbian Democratic Party to run in the elections and to put forth some other candidates on its behalf. So this is not the list of the candidates that were running in the election.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You, nevertheless, accept that that is your name which appears on a list which is described as a list of candidates for the SDS?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Listen, I was not on the list of candidates running for MPs in Novi Grad municipality. It doesn't make sense for a list of future MPs to contain the names of a hundred candidates. What I'm saying here, what I'm telling you, is the truth and it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, Mr. President. We'll upload an English translation as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now I'd like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P5975, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to the origins of the Serb municipality of Rajlovac. First, before we get there, as a member of the SDS you did share the views of the SDS, did you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Those views included defended the interests of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Defending the territories of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Well, what period of time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to the period of time from 1990 all the way up until 1995 for the purpose of that question.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Until the combat activities started, we did not need to defend the territory of the Serbian people. It was only when we came under threat that we started defending the Serbian territory. Before that, Rajlovac municipality, where I resided was used by the larger municipality Novi Grad, Sarajevo. In Rajlovac municipality, only economic reasons were in place for Rajlovac municipality to separate from Novi Grad Sarajevo municipality. Nobody thought of war at that time. In Rajlovac municipality there were a lot of large companies that had large profits. For example, I can tell you the names of all of them, but let me give you just a few of them. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, Mr. Witness, can I suggest --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Did you not understand me?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I understand you, Mr. Witness. Can I ask you to focus on the questions which are put to you, and subject to a direction from the Trial Chamber try and keep your answers a little shorter and more focused. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Well, I didn't understand you then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you accept that preparations for the establishment of the Serb municipality of Rajlovac started in around October 1991?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: I really don't know when that happened. I'm not sure of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Approximately what date would you say that the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac was established?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The name of the municipality was the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: I don't know, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your evidence is that you do not know what the formal name of the -- that the formal name of Rajlovac of the municipal entity that was created was the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac. Is it your evidence that you don't know that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: I wasn't -- I don't have a clue. I don't know whether the prefix "Srpska" preceded the name. I was not interested in that. It was Rajlovac municipality. It is possible. Now it has just occurred to me. There was a stamp, but I don't know whether that was the full title featured on that stamp. But if you say so, then I suppose you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's not me testifying, sir. At paragraph 68 of your statement, which is -- appears on page 18 you state: "In the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac which is at the same time the zone of responsibility of my brigade, there was no persecution policy on religious or ethnic grounds." You can consult the relevant page of your statement. My question to you is: Why was it called the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: I apologise, I apologise. What paragraph are you referring me to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sixty-eight.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Prosecutor, sir, maybe we are talking at cross-purposes here. When Rajlovac municipality was founded, I don't know whether it had the prefix "Serbian" in its name. Later on it became commonplace. That's why I used it. The way I understood your question was whether the prefix "Srpski" was used from the very outset, from the moment when Rajlovac municipality was established. Later on, especially during the conflict, it became a common practice to call it the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And why was it called the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Well, I haven't a clue. I suppose because Serbs resided in that municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your paragraph at -- statement at paragraph 6 you give some figures from the 1991 census, and you say that there were 1.066 Muslims living in the local commune of Dobrosevici. That's paragraphs 5 and 6. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Of those 1066 Muslims, approximately how many were in Ahatovici would you say?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: A majority, perhaps a half, I don't know, or maybe even more than half.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, going back to paragraphs 68, you refer to a number of non-Serb people living in the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac. And before we get there, is it true that the village of Ahatovici was encompassed within the territory of the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In paragraph 68 you note the existence of three Croatian families and three individuals who were Muslims and you name those three individuals in paragraph 68. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, my question to you is: What happened to the 1.066 Muslims who lived in the Dobrosevici area before the war? Why were there only three Muslims in the municipality -- Serbian municipality of Rajlovac by the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: No, what I was talking about is not the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac, but Dobrosevici local commune. Second of all, after the 4th of June, 1992, after fighting in Ahatovici, the Muslim population surrendered to the Serbian military and the civilian population expressed a wish to leave and go to Sarajevo and they left. And those were not only three Croatian families, not the only three Croatian families. Actually, there were a woman and her parents. Their family name was Pasic. And those were not just the Rebo, Martinovic, Bosnjak families, the names applied to several families and I don't know their exact numbers. Almost all of them from those Croatian families stayed. Younger people left because they were probably afraid they would be recruited to the Army of Republika Srpska. Nobody actually touched them. They left of their own free will. As for the Pasic family, that covers several families who resided in some dozen houses. They left of their own free will because of some problems. They resided above the Butile barracks. Fire was opened from their houses at the barracks. I don't know how they were moved into some dozen weekend cottages, but I know that they left the area of their own free will and that they left in the direction of Kiseljak. On several occasions I popped over and visited them because they resided close to where I lived. Our relations were good. I asked them if they needed anything. They lived there and they enjoyed all the rights like any other citizen. They couldn't go to their own houses. That was the only exception. They had to report to somebody from the military police --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: -- I don't know who that was --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction in the transcript. Let us clarify whether fire was opened from the barracks at those houses or whether it was the other way around; i.e., whether fire was opened from those houses at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That can be corrected in re-direct I would suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very much so. Please continue. But Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the witness said that fire was opened from the houses. I have an objection to the transcript. Why don't you clarify with the witness now and ask him what he actually said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Transcription or transcript can be corrected later on by -- if there's a proper request. I couldn't find the passage here so that's why I suggested continuing with the evidence. I find the flow of evidence very important. Mr. Dzino, because what you are saying has to be interpreted in two languages, please speak slowly. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 15, if I may be of assistance. On line 15 the witness's words were misrecorded. That's on page 104.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That will be checked against the recording by the CLSS. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, in your -- one of your answers you referred to the Muslim civilians from Ahatovici surrendering to Serb forces. Can we agree that that was in late May 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: I know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is the exact date?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: It started on the 31st of May and lasted until the 2nd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Their Honours have received evidence, the citations are P2314, paragraph 46; and P2310, paragraphs 31 to 33. The Judges have received evidence that hundreds of Muslim women, children, and men from Ahatovici and its surrounding villages were detained in several locations in Rajlovac following the take-over of Ahatovici by Serb forces. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: I know that they were detained, but I don't know where nor how. Not only were they detained, I would like you to show me a map. When we are talking about Ahatovici, there's only the Ahatovici local commune which was inhabited by Muslims. The extremists who wanted to engage in fighting were in Ahatovici. The lower-lying areas, I'm speaking off the top of my head, it would be best to see the map then you would understand what I'm talking about. I don't know how things transpired. In any case, those people did not engage in major fighting. They surrendered. And I know for a fact that some of the men, for example, the Gacanovici [phoen] family asked their neighbours to drive them to some -- Revo [phoen]. They never arrived in Rajlovica. As for the civilians from Ahatovici, more specifically the villages in Ahatovici which composed one-third of the local commune, they were indeed taken to Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And are you aware that many were treated to beatings? They were kept in inhumane conditions. Several were beaten to death according to the evidence the Trial Chamber has received. Have you heard anything about that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: I'm sorry that that happened. I really was not in Rajlovac at the time, nor do I know what happened there, and if what you're saying indeed did happen I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, just one or two questions. We need to rise at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly. We can stop there. Thank you, Mr. President. It's -- this is an appropriate place to stop as far as my planning is concerned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll rise today and we'll continue tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 7th day of November, 2012, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
